questions.stem: Salt water is heated in simple distillation. What is collected in the beaker, and what is left in the flask?

options.text: Pure water collects in the beaker; the salt stays in the flask
options.explanation: Only the liquid boils off and condenses; the dissolved solid cannot evaporate.

options.text: Salt collects in the beaker; water stays in the flask
options.explanation: The vapour that rises is water, so water is what the condenser delivers to the beaker.

options.text: Both collect in the beaker as salt water
options.explanation: Distillation separates; the beaker receives the condensed liquid only.

options.text: Nothing collects until the salt boils too
options.explanation: Heating stops once the liquid has gone; the salt never boils.

questions.stem: In a labelled diagram of simple distillation, where must the cooling water enter?

options.text: At the bottom of the condenser, near the collecting beaker
options.explanation: Water entering low fills the cooling jacket against the vapour flow and chills the whole condenser.

options.text: At the top of the condenser, near the column
options.explanation: That is where water leaves; entering high leaves the lower jacket uncooled.

options.text: Into the flask, to speed the boiling
options.explanation: Cooling water belongs to the condenser jacket, not the boiling flask.

options.text: Anywhere, since the direction makes no difference
options.explanation: Diagrams are marked on the correct direction, as the exam hint stresses.

questions.stem: Ethanol and water mix completely. Which technique separates them, and how is it run?

options.text: Fractional distillation: hold 78 °C to boil off the ethanol, then stop before 100 °C
options.explanation: The lower boiling point leaves first; stopping at 100 °C keeps water out of the beaker.

options.text: Filtration: ethanol passes through, water is caught
options.explanation: Both are liquids; there is no undissolved solid for filter paper to catch.

options.text: Simple distillation: collect both liquids in one beaker
options.explanation: One beaker of mixed distillate is no separation at all.

options.text: Crystallisation: cool until ethanol crystals form
options.explanation: Ethanol does not crystallise from the mixture; it boils at 78 °C.

questions.stem: During fractional distillation of ethanol and water, the thermometer climbs from 78 °C towards 100 °C. What should the operator do?

options.text: Stop heating — the ethanol has all been collected
options.explanation: A rising temperature means the low-boiling substance is gone and water is next.

options.text: Increase the heat to finish faster
options.explanation: More heat brings water over and ruins the separation.

options.text: Swap the beaker and keep collecting the same liquid
options.explanation: The distillate is already the ethanol; continuing collects water into it.

options.text: Add cold water to the mixture
options.explanation: Dilution does not separate anything.

questions.stem: What does miscible mean, and why does it rule out filtration for an ethanol-water mixture?

options.text: The liquids mix with no boundary, so no solid exists for filter paper to catch
options.explanation: Filtration needs an undissolved solid; two liquids that blend have none.

options.text: The liquids have equal densities, so they cannot be separated at all
options.explanation: Density equality is irrelevant; boiling points do the separating.

options.text: The liquids react into a compound, so distillation is barred
options.explanation: Miscible liquids still blend physically; nothing new is formed.

options.text: The liquids must first be frozen to separate them
options.explanation: The separation runs on boiling point differences, not freezing.

questions.stem: Sand is stirred into water. Which technique recovers the sand, and what is the sand left on the paper called?

options.text: Filtration; the sand left on the paper is the residue
options.explanation: Undissolved solids stay on the paper as residue while the filtrate passes.

options.text: Filtration; the sand in the beaker below is the filtrate
options.explanation: The filtrate is the liquid that passed through, not the solid caught.

options.text: Simple distillation; the sand boils off first
options.explanation: Sand is a solid with no boiling point to exploit here.

options.text: Crystallisation; the sand grows crystals
options.explanation: Crystals grow from dissolved solids; sand never dissolved.

questions.stem: How does a cold glass rod test whether a solution is ready for crystallisation?

options.text: Dip a clean, dry, cold rod in; crystals forming on it show the solution is saturated
options.explanation: A saturated solution deposits crystals on a cold surface straight away.

options.text: The rod dissolves if the solution is saturated
options.explanation: Glass does not dissolve; the rod is an observation tool.

options.text: The rod changes colour when crystals are near
options.explanation: The signal is crystal growth on the rod, not a colour change.

options.text: Stir with the rod; faster stirring proves saturation
options.explanation: Stirring changes nothing about how much is dissolved.

questions.stem: Why does crystallisation need a solid that is much more soluble in hot solvent than in cold?

options.text: The gap lets crystals grow as the solution cools and keeps them from redissolving
options.explanation: Falling solubility on cooling drives the solid out of solution as crystals.

options.text: Hot solvent sterilises the crystals
options.explanation: The technique rests on solubility differences, not hygiene.

options.text: Cold solvent would boil instead
options.explanation: Cooling is applied after heating; nothing boils during crystallisation.

options.text: The solid must melt before it can crystallise
options.explanation: Crystals form from solution; melting the solid is not part of the method.

questions.stem: In paper chromatography, why must the pencil line sit above the solvent level at the start?

options.text: So the samples do not wash off the line into the solvent container
options.explanation: Submerged spots dissolve away into the solvent instead of travelling up the paper.

options.text: So the solvent cannot evaporate
options.explanation: Line placement has no effect on evaporation.

options.text: So the pencil does not run into the chromatogram
options.explanation: Pencil is chosen precisely because it does not run; the depth rule protects the samples.

options.text: Because spots below the line travel faster
options.explanation: Travel distance depends on solubility, not on starting depth.

questions.stem: Why is the starting line drawn in pencil rather than ink?

options.text: Pencil does not dissolve, so it will not run up the paper with the samples
options.explanation: Ink would travel with the solvent and confuse the results.

options.text: Pencil marks are darker and easier to see
options.explanation: Visibility is not the reason; chemical inertness in the solvent is.

options.text: Ink would make the paper too heavy
options.explanation: Paper mass is irrelevant.

options.text: Pencil is the only colour allowed under exam rules
options.explanation: The rule is chemical: inks dissolve and would join the separation.
